topic: Mastering the Change of Basis in Linear Algebra

sections.title: Prerequisite Review: Coordinate Systems as Languages
lecture_lines: Basis vectors form our coordinate language.
Changing basis changes the grid lines.
Positions are defined by relative basis units.
animations: 1. Create a square grid coordinate system in #FFFFFF color and label it 'Basis B'.
2. Show a point labeled 'Cat' at position (2, 3) relative to 'Basis B'.
3. Transition to a skewed grid in #FFFF00 color and label it 'Basis B''.
4. Maintain the 'Cat' position while updating the coordinate values relative to 'Basis B''.
5. Highlight the difference between the two coordinate representations for the same point.

sections.title: Defining the Transition Matrix
lecture_lines: Columns of P are new basis vectors.
animations: 1. Draw two sets of vectors: Set A in #FF0000 and Set B in #00FF00.
2. Construct a Matrix P with the columns representing vectors from Set B in terms of Set A.
3. Represent P as a 'Bridge' object connecting B-coordinates to A-coordinates.
4. Show a vector v in B-coordinates input into P.
5. Show the transformation resulting in v in A-coordinates as output.

sections.title: The Mechanism: How to Calculate
lecture_lines: Step 2: Place them as columns in P.
Step 3: Multiply P by coordinate vector.
animations: 1. Display text steps '1. Identify B and B'', '2. Form P', '3. Calculate'.
2. Show 'Robot-Basis' vectors as columns to form matrix P.
3. Illustrate the multiplication process: P * [v_robot] = [v_world].
4. Show the robot arm extending to pick up an item at [v_world].
5. Use a checkmark to signify the successful conversion of coordinates.

sections.title: Summary & Geometric Intuition
lecture_lines: Change of basis is space relabelling.
The vector itself stays the same.
P-inverse converts back to original basis.
animations: 1. Split screen view: Left panel shows point fixed, right panel shows point values changing.
2. Animate the 'Basis' rotating on the left while coordinates remain static.
3. Animate the values [x, y] updating on the right for the same static point.
4. Introduce P^-1 and show it reversing the transformation back to standard.
5. Conclude with both viewpoints labeled 'Same Point, Different Language'.
